claim: Fragile X syndrome (FXS) is an X chromosome-linked disease associated with severe intellectual disabilities.
source: Fragile X syndrome (FXS) is an X chromosome-linked disease associated with severe intellectual disabilities.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the scientific literature about FXS, representing general knowledge in the field.

claim: The efficacy of hippocampal engram reactivation is reduced in Fmr1 KO mice performing contextual fear memory recall.
source: Here, we show that the efficacy of hippocampal engram reactivation is reduced in Fmr1 KO mice performing contextual fear memory recall.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2E showing reduced engram reactivation efficacy in Fmr1 KO mice compared to WT.

claim: Experiencing an enriched environment (EE) prior to learning improved the engram reactivation efficacy in Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Experiencing an enriched environment (EE) prior to learning improved the engram reactivation efficacy and rescued memory recall in the Fmr1 KO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I demonstrating that EE experience restores engram reactivation efficacy to wild-type levels in Fmr1 KO mice.

claim: Experiencing an enriched environment (EE) prior to learning rescued memory recall in Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Experiencing an enriched environment (EE) prior to learning improved the engram reactivation efficacy and rescued memory recall in the Fmr1 KO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data in Figure 3C showing that EE experience normalized freezing behavior during contextual memory recall in Fmr1 KO mice.

claim: Chemogenetically inhibiting EE-engaged neurons in CA1 reverses the rescue effect of EE on memory recall.
source: In addition, chemogenetically inhibiting EE-engaged neurons in CA1 reverses the rescue effect of EE on memory recall.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5H showing that DREADD-mediated inhibition of EE-activated neurons abolished the memory rescue effect in Fmr1 KO mice.

claim: Inappropriate engram reactivation underlies cognitive deficits in FXS.
source: Thus, our results suggest that inappropriate engram reactivation underlies cognitive deficits in FXS, and enriched environment may rescue cognitive deficits by improving network activation accuracy.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the correlation between reduced engram reactivation efficacy and impaired memory recall shown in Figure 2E and 2F.

claim: Enriched environment may rescue cognitive deficits by improving network activation accuracy.
source: Thus, our results suggest that inappropriate engram reactivation underlies cognitive deficits in FXS, and enriched environment may rescue cognitive deficits by improving network activation accuracy.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on data showing that EE improves engram reactivation efficacy (Figure 3I) and rescues memory recall (Figure 3C).

claim: FXS is a neurodevelopmental disorder associated with intellectual disability.
source: Fragile X syndrome (FXS) is a neurodevelopmental disorder associated with intellectual disability and a leading genetic cause of syndromic autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) (Santoro et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Santoro et al., 2012.

claim: FXS is a leading genetic cause of syndromic autism spectrum disorders (ASDs).
source: Fragile X syndrome (FXS) is a neurodevelopmental disorder associated with intellectual disability and a leading genetic cause of syndromic autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) (Santoro et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Santoro et al., 2012.

claim: FXS is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the fragile X mental retardation 1 (FMR1) gene.
source: FXS is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the fragile X mental retardation 1 (FMR1) gene, which encodes the fragile X mental retardation protein (FMRP) (Verkerk et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Verkerk et al., 1991.

claim: The FMR1 gene encodes the fragile X mental retardation protein (FMRP).
source: FXS is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the fragile X mental retardation 1 (FMR1) gene, which encodes the fragile X mental retardation protein (FMRP) (Verkerk et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Verkerk et al., 1991.

claim: The most common cause of FXS is the expansion of CGG trinucleotide repeats within the 5′ untranslated region of the FMR1 gene.
source: The most common cause of FXS is the expansion of CGG trinucleotide repeats within the 5′ untranslated region of the FMR1 gene, which triggers hypermethylation of the CpG island in the promoter region and subsequent silencing of the FMR1 gene, resulting in the loss of FMRP expression (Fu et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fu et al., 1991.

claim: CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion triggers hypermethylation of the CpG island in the FMR1 promoter region.
source: The most common cause of FXS is the expansion of CGG trinucleotide repeats within the 5′ untranslated region of the FMR1 gene, which triggers hypermethylation of the CpG island in the promoter region and subsequent silencing of the FMR1 gene, resulting in the loss of FMRP expression (Fu et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fu et al., 1991.

claim: Hypermethylation of the CpG island in the FMR1 promoter region leads to subsequent silencing of the FMR1 gene.
source: The most common cause of FXS is the expansion of CGG trinucleotide repeats within the 5′ untranslated region of the FMR1 gene, which triggers hypermethylation of the CpG island in the promoter region and subsequent silencing of the FMR1 gene, resulting in the loss of FMRP expression (Fu et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fu et al., 1991.

claim: Silencing of the FMR1 gene results in the loss of FMRP expression.
source: The most common cause of FXS is the expansion of CGG trinucleotide repeats within the 5′ untranslated region of the FMR1 gene, which triggers hypermethylation of the CpG island in the promoter region and subsequent silencing of the FMR1 gene, resulting in the loss of FMRP expression (Fu et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fu et al., 1991.

claim: Other loss-of-function mutations in the FMR1 coding region have been identified in rare cases of FXS.
source: Other loss-of-function mutations in the FMR1 coding region have also been identified in rare cases of FXS (Suhl and Warren, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Suhl and Warren, 2015.

claim: FMRP is an RNA-binding protein.
source: As an RNA-binding protein, FMRP interacts with and regulates the translation of a large number of mRNAs encoding proteins involved in regulation of neuronal morphology and synaptic function (Ascano et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ascano et al., 2012.

claim: FMRP interacts with and regulates the translation of a large number of mRNAs encoding proteins involved in regulation of neuronal morphology and synaptic function.
source: As an RNA-binding protein, FMRP interacts with and regulates the translation of a large number of mRNAs encoding proteins involved in regulation of neuronal morphology and synaptic function (Ascano et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ascano et al., 2012.

claim: In the absence of FMRP, dysregulated protein synthesis affects multiple neuronal pathways.
source: Thus, in the absence of FMRP, dysregulated protein synthesis affects multiple neuronal pathways, generating behavioral phenotypes displayed by FXS patients, such as repetitive behavior and impaired cognitive functions and social interactions (Bagni et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bagni et al., 2012.

claim: Dysregulated protein synthesis in the absence of FMRP generates behavioral phenotypes displayed by FXS patients, such as repetitive behavior and impaired cognitive functions and social interactions.
source: Thus, in the absence of FMRP, dysregulated protein synthesis affects multiple neuronal pathways, generating behavioral phenotypes displayed by FXS patients, such as repetitive behavior and impaired cognitive functions and social interactions (Bagni et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bagni et al., 2012.

claim: A FXS mouse model with constitutive deletion of the Fmr1 gene (Fmr1 KO) has been used extensively to study neural mechanisms underlying cognitive impairments of FXS patients.
source: A FXS mouse model with constitutive deletion of the Fmr1 gene (Fmr1 KO) has been used extensively to study neural mechanisms underlying cognitive impairments of FXS patients (Bakker et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bakker et al., 1994.

claim: Results and conclusions from some of the behavioral tests conducted in Fmr1 KO mice remain controversial.
source: Although results and conclusions from some of the behavioral tests conducted in these animals remain controversial (Kazdoba et al., 2014), the Fmr1 KO mouse nonetheless recapitulates most of the behavioral characteristics displayed by FXS patients, including deficits in learning and memory (Krueger et al., 2011; Santos et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kazdoba et al., 2014.

claim: The Fmr1 KO mouse recapitulates most of the behavioral characteristics displayed by FXS patients, including deficits in learning and memory.
source: Although results and conclusions from some of the behavioral tests conducted in these animals remain controversial (Kazdoba et al., 2014), the Fmr1 KO mouse nonetheless recapitulates most of the behavioral characteristics displayed by FXS patients, including deficits in learning and memory (Krueger et al., 2011; Santos et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Krueger et al., 2011 and Santos et al., 2014.

claim: Synaptic plasticity changes often underly learning deficits in animal models of neurological diseases.
source: Synaptic plasticity changes are often found to underly learning deficits in animal models of neurological diseases.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established knowledge in the field of neuroscience.

claim: Fmr1 KO mice exhibit various synaptic dysfunctions associated with FMRP deletion.
source: Indeed, Fmr1 KO mice exhibit various synaptic dysfunctions associated with FMRP deletion (Contractor et al., 2015; Pfeiffer and Huber, 2009), including excessive group 1 mGluR-dependent long-term depression (mGluR-LTD) (Hou et al., 2006; Huber et al., 2002; Koekkoek et al., 2005), abnormal long-term potentiation (LTP) (Lauterborn et al., 2007; Martin et al., 2016; Paradee et al., 1999; Tian et al., 2017), and impaired homeostatic synaptic plasticity (Sarti et al., 2013; Soden and Chen, 2010; Zhong et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to Contractor et al., 2015 and Pfeiffer and Huber, 2009.

claim: Fmr1 KO mice exhibit excessive group 1 mGluR-dependent long-term depression (mGluR-LTD).
source: Indeed, Fmr1 KO mice exhibit various synaptic dysfunctions associated with FMRP deletion (Contractor et al., 2015; Pfeiffer and Huber, 2009), including excessive group 1 mGluR-dependent long-term depression (mGluR-LTD) (Hou et al., 2006; Huber et al., 2002; Koekkoek et al., 2005), abnormal long-term potentiation (LTP) (Lauterborn et al., 2007; Martin et al., 2016; Paradee et al., 1999; Tian et al., 2017), and impaired homeostatic synaptic plasticity (Sarti et al., 2013; Soden and Chen, 2010; Zhong et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hou et al., 2006; Huber et al., 2002; Koekkoek et al., 2005.

claim: Fmr1 KO mice exhibit abnormal long-term potentiation (LTP).
source: Indeed, Fmr1 KO mice exhibit various synaptic dysfunctions associated with FMRP deletion (Contractor et al., 2015; Pfeiffer and Huber, 2009), including excessive group 1 mGluR-dependent long-term depression (mGluR-LTD) (Hou et al., 2006; Huber et al., 2002; Koekkoek et al., 2005), abnormal long-term potentiation (LTP) (Lauterborn et al., 2007; Martin et al., 2016; Paradee et al., 1999; Tian et al., 2017), and impaired homeostatic synaptic plasticity (Sarti et al., 2013; Soden and Chen, 2010; Zhong et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lauterborn et al., 2007; Martin et al., 2016; Paradee et al., 1999; Tian et al., 2017.

claim: Fmr1 KO mice exhibit impaired homeostatic synaptic plasticity.
source: Indeed, Fmr1 KO mice exhibit various synaptic dysfunctions associated with FMRP deletion (Contractor et al., 2015; Pfeiffer and Huber, 2009), including excessive group 1 mGluR-dependent long-term depression (mGluR-LTD) (Hou et al., 2006; Huber et al., 2002; Koekkoek et al., 2005), abnormal long-term potentiation (LTP) (Lauterborn et al., 2007; Martin et al., 2016; Paradee et al., 1999; Tian et al., 2017), and impaired homeostatic synaptic plasticity (Sarti et al., 2013; Soden and Chen, 2010; Zhong et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sarti et al., 2013; Soden and Chen, 2010; Zhong et al., 2018.

claim: Impaired homeostatic synaptic plasticity has been validated in human neurons differentiated from FXS patient iPS cells.
source: Some of these findings, such as impaired homeostatic synaptic plasticity, has been validated in human neurons differentiated from FXS patient iPS cells (Zhang et al., 2018), indicating that they are translationally relevant.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: Findings from Fmr1 KO mice are translationally relevant.
source: Some of these findings, such as impaired homeostatic synaptic plasticity, has been validated in human neurons differentiated from FXS patient iPS cells (Zhang et al., 2018), indicating that they are translationally relevant.
evidence: This is an inference based on validation in human neurons from FXS patient iPS cells.

claim: Network activation patterns relevant to memory formation may be affected by synaptic dysfunction in FXS.
source: These results provide a strong correlation between altered synaptic function and memory deficits in FXS and predict that network activation patterns relevant to memory formation may be affected by synaptic dysfunction, thus contributing to learning deficits exhibited in behaving animals.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the correlation between synaptic dysfunction and memory deficits.

claim: Fmr1 KO mice exhibited normal learning during fear conditioning training.
source: In both behavioral tasks, Fmr1 KO mice exhibited normal learning, indicated by their normal performance during and immediately after training (Figure 1A and C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1A, 1C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Fmr1 KO mice exhibited impaired memory recall 1–3 days after training in contextual fear conditioning.
source: By contrast, their memory recall 1–3 days after training was significantly impaired in both tasks (Figure 1B and D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1B and 1D.

claim: Fmr1 KO mice showed no deficits in pain perception.
source: Hot plate test revealed no deficits in pain perception in the Fmr1 KO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that impaired memory is not likely due to compromised pain perception.
evidence: This is supported by data from hot plate test shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Impaired memory in Fmr1 KO mice is not likely due to compromised pain perception.
source: Hot plate test revealed no deficits in pain perception in the Fmr1 KO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that impaired memory is not likely due to compromised pain perception.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of pain perception deficits shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Fmr1 KO mice performed similarly to their WT littermates in Y maze.
source: Additionally, Fmr1 KO mice performed similarly to their WT littermates in Y maze, open field test, elevated plus maze and novel object recognition test (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F), indicating that their working memory, locomotion, non-social anxiety levels and hippocampus-independent recognition memory are all normal.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Fmr1 KO mice performed similarly to their WT littermates in open field test.
source: Additionally, Fmr1 KO mice performed similarly to their WT littermates in Y maze, open field test, elevated plus maze and novel object recognition test (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F), indicating that their working memory, locomotion, non-social anxiety levels and hippocampus-independent recognition memory are all normal.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Fmr1 KO mice performed similarly to their WT littermates in elevated plus maze.
source: Additionally, Fmr1 KO mice performed similarly to their WT littermates in Y maze, open field test, elevated plus maze and novel object recognition test (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F), indicating that their working memory, locomotion, non-social anxiety levels and hippocampus-independent recognition memory are all normal.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Fmr1 KO mice performed similarly to their WT littermates in novel object recognition test.
source: Additionally, Fmr1 KO mice performed similarly to their WT littermates in Y maze, open field test, elevated plus maze and novel object recognition test (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F), indicating that their working memory, locomotion, non-social anxiety levels and hippocampus-independent recognition memory are all normal.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Working memory is normal in Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Additionally, Fmr1 KO mice performed similarly to their WT littermates in Y maze, open field test, elevated plus maze and novel object recognition test (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F), indicating that their working memory, locomotion, non-social anxiety levels and hippocampus-independent recognition memory are all normal.
evidence: This is inferred from normal performance in Y maze test shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Locomotion is normal in Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Additionally, Fmr1 KO mice performed similarly to their WT littermates in Y maze, open field test, elevated plus maze and novel object recognition test (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F), indicating that their working memory, locomotion, non-social anxiety levels and hippocampus-independent recognition memory are all normal.
evidence: This is inferred from normal performance in open field test shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Non-social anxiety levels are normal in Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Additionally, Fmr1 KO mice performed similarly to their WT littermates in Y maze, open field test, elevated plus maze and novel object recognition test (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F), indicating that their working memory, locomotion, non-social anxiety levels and hippocampus-independent recognition memory are all normal.
evidence: This is inferred from normal performance in elevated plus maze shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Hippocampus-independent recognition memory is normal in Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Additionally, Fmr1 KO mice performed similarly to their WT littermates in Y maze, open field test, elevated plus maze and novel object recognition test (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F), indicating that their working memory, locomotion, non-social anxiety levels and hippocampus-independent recognition memory are all normal.
evidence: This is inferred from normal performance in novel object recognition test shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: CA1-Fmr1 KO mice showed normal performance during and after training of conventional fear conditioning paradigm.
source: The CA1-Fmr1 KO mice showed normal performance during and after training of conventional fear conditioning paradigm (one session of three tone-foot shock pairs) (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1H), but exhibited contextual memory deficits tested one day after training (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: CA1-Fmr1 KO mice exhibited contextual memory deficits tested one day after training.
source: The CA1-Fmr1 KO mice showed normal performance during and after training of conventional fear conditioning paradigm (one session of three tone-foot shock pairs) (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1H), but exhibited contextual memory deficits tested one day after training (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: CA1-Fmr1 KO mice showed no deficit on pain perception, working memory, locomotion, anxiety, and object recognition memory.
source: No deficit on pain perception, working memory, locomotion, anxiety, and object recognition memory were observed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I–L).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I–L.

claim: Normal expression of FMRP in hippocampal CA1 is required for contextual memory formation.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that normal expression of FMRP in hippocampal CA1 is required for contextual memory formation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that CA1-specific FMRP deletion leads to contextual memory deficits (Figure 1G).

claim: Both fear conditioning training and memory recall activated comparable numbers of neurons in CA1 in both WT and Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Both fear conditioning training and memory recall activated comparable numbers of neurons in CA1 in both WT and Fmr1 KO mice, indicated by similar percentage of tdTomato-expressing (training-activated) and FOS-positive (memory recall-activated) neurons in these mice (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: A significantly higher portion of the tdTomato-positive neurons expressed FOS compared to tdTomato-negative neurons in both WT and KO mice.
source: Additionally, compared to tdTomato-negative neurons, a significantly higher portion of the tdTomato-positive neurons expressed FOS in both WT and KO mice, suggesting that learning-labeled memory engrams were preferentially reactivated during memory recall, consistent with their predicted roles in memory encoding (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Learning-labeled memory engrams were preferentially reactivated during memory recall.
source: Additionally, compared to tdTomato-negative neurons, a significantly higher portion of the tdTomato-positive neurons expressed FOS in both WT and KO mice, suggesting that learning-labeled memory engrams were preferentially reactivated during memory recall, consistent with their predicted roles in memory encoding (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the higher FOS expression in tdTomato-positive neurons shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Preferential reactivation of engrams is significantly reduced in Fmr1 KO mice compared to WT.
source: However, compared to WT, this preferential reactivation is significantly reduced in Fmr1 KO mice (Figure 2E), suggesting that reactivation efficacy is decreased in the Fmr1 KO mice.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Reactivation efficacy is decreased in the Fmr1 KO mice.
source: However, compared to WT, this preferential reactivation is significantly reduced in Fmr1 KO mice (Figure 2E), suggesting that reactivation efficacy is decreased in the Fmr1 KO mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reduced preferential reactivation shown in Figure 2E.

claim: CA1 engram reactivation efficacy is positively correlated with animal's performance during context memory test.
source: Further, the Pearson correlation analysis of individual animal's freezing levels during recall and their CA1 engram reactivation efficacy showed a significant correlation between the two measurements (Figure 2F), indicating that CA1 engram reactivation efficacy is positively correlated with animal's performance during context memory test.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Enriched environment (EE) has been shown to improve cognitive function and ameliorate some symptoms of neurodevelopmental disorders.
source: Enriched environment (EE) experience, which provides rich sensory, motor, and social stimulation to mice, has been shown to improve cognitive function and ameliorate some symptoms of neurodevelopmental disorders (Nithianantharajah and Hannan, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nithianantharajah and Hannan, 2006.

claim: EE has been shown to correct dendritic morphological abnormalities in FXS mice.
source: In FXS mice, EE has been shown to correct dendritic morphological abnormalities and rescue behavioral phenotypes of hyperactivity, social deficits and performances in some cognitive tasks (Oddi et al., 2015; Restivo et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Oddi et al., 2015 and Restivo et al., 2005.

claim: EE has been shown to rescue behavioral phenotypes of hyperactivity, social deficits and performances in some cognitive tasks in FXS mice.
source: In FXS mice, EE has been shown to correct dendritic morphological abnormalities and rescue behavioral phenotypes of hyperactivity, social deficits and performances in some cognitive tasks (Oddi et al., 2015; Restivo et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Oddi et al., 2015 and Restivo et al., 2005.

claim: Fmr1 KO mice showed normal freezing during learning when trained with the intensive fear conditioning paradigm after EE experience.
source: Similar to home cage-raised mice, Fmr1 KO mice showed normal freezing during learning when trained with the intensive fear conditioning paradigm (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: EE experience fully reversed fear memory deficit in Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Moreover, EE experience fully reversed fear memory deficit in Fmr1 KO mice as they exhibited normal freezing behavior during contextual memory recall 3 days after the training (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The rescue effect by EE in Fmr1 KO mice learning was also apparent in the passive avoidance test.
source: The rescue effect by EE in Fmr1 KO mice learning was also apparent in the passive avoidance test done in a separate cohort of mice (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: Nociception, working memory, locomotion, object recognition memory, and non-social anxiety levels were not affected by EE.
source: Nociception, working memory, locomotion, object recognition memory, and non-social anxiety levels were not affected by EE (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–F.

claim: Engram reactivation efficacy in Fmr1 KO CA1 was improved by EE to wild-type levels.
source: We next examined memory engram reactivation in Fmr1 KO mice after EE experience. Corroborating the behavioral results, engram reactivation efficacy in Fmr1 KO CA1 was also improved by EE to wild-type levels without significantly changing the overall CA1 activation levels during learning or memory recall (Figure 3F–J).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3F–J.

claim: EE did not significantly change the overall CA1 activation levels during learning or memory recall.
source: We next examined memory engram reactivation in Fmr1 KO mice after EE experience. Corroborating the behavioral results, engram reactivation efficacy in Fmr1 KO CA1 was also improved by EE to wild-type levels without significantly changing the overall CA1 activation levels during learning or memory recall (Figure 3F–J).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3G and 3H.

claim: EE experience rescues fear memory deficits in the Fmr1 KO mouse by improving the engram reactivation efficacy during memory recall.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that EE experience rescues fear memory deficits in the Fmr1 KO mouse by improving the engram reactivation efficacy during memory recall.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined behavioral and engram reactivation data shown in Figure 3.

claim: EE extensively activated neurons in CA1, as roughly 25% neurons were labeled by tdTomato in both WT and KO groups.
source: EE extensively activated neurons in CA1, as roughly 25% neurons were labeled by tdTomato in both WT and KO groups (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Immunolabeling with FOS showed comparable degrees of neuronal activation in CA1 by 1 hr and 10 day EE experience in WT and Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Immunolabeling with FOS showed comparable degrees of neuronal activation in CA1 by 1 hr and 10 day EE experience in WT and Fmr1 KO mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C), indicating that absence of FMRP does not affect neuron engagement during EE.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Absence of FMRP does not affect neuron engagement during EE.
source: Immunolabeling with FOS showed comparable degrees of neuronal activation in CA1 by 1 hr and 10 day EE experience in WT and Fmr1 KO mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C), indicating that absence of FMRP does not affect neuron engagement during EE.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparable FOS expression shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Overall CA1 engagement during fear learning was similar (~20%) between both WT and KO mice.
source: Overall CA1 engagement during fear learning was similar (~20%) between both WT and KO mice (Figure 4B and D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4B and 4D.

claim: Compared to tdTomato- neurons, tdTomato+ neurons showed a four-fold increase in FOS expression.
source: Interestingly, compared to tdTomato- neurons (not engaged in EE), which had very low FOS expression (~10%), tdTomato+ neurons (EE-activated) showed a four-fold increase in FOS expression, indicating that fear learning preferentially recruited EE-activated neurons (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Fear learning preferentially recruited EE-activated neurons.
source: Interestingly, compared to tdTomato- neurons (not engaged in EE), which had very low FOS expression (~10%), tdTomato+ neurons (EE-activated) showed a four-fold increase in FOS expression, indicating that fear learning preferentially recruited EE-activated neurons (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the higher FOS expression in tdTomato+ neurons shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Fear learning preferentially recruited EE-activated neurons in both WT and Fmr1 KO CA1.
source: This is the case for both WT and Fmr1 KO CA1 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: A behaviorally relevant activity history (i.e. activation during EE) facilitates the likelihood of a neuron to participate in subsequent learning tasks.
source: Thus, a behaviorally relevant activity history (i.e. activation during EE) facilitates the likelihood of a neuron to participate in subsequent learning tasks.
evidence: This is an inference based on the preferential recruitment of EE-activated neurons during learning shown in Figure 4E.

claim: DREADD expression did not affect tdTomato labeling of EE-activated neurons in either WT or Fmr1 KO mice.
source: As expected, DREADD expression did not affect tdTomato labeling of EE-activated neurons in either WT or Fmr1 KO mice (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: Normal freezing behavior during training and similar levels of CA1 activation were observed in control and DREADD-expressing WT and Fmr1 KO mice trained by conventional fear conditioning paradigm.
source: Additionally, normal freezing behavior during training and similar levels of CA1 activation were observed in control and DREADD-expressing WT and Fmr1 KO mice trained by conventional fear conditioning paradigm (Figure 5B and D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B, 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claim: DREADD expression in EE-activated neurons significantly dampened their participation in subsequent learning in both WT and Fmr1 KO neurons.
source: A closer look showed that DREADD expression in EE-activated neurons significantly dampened their participation in subsequent learning in both WT and Fmr1 KO neurons, indicated by a significant shift of FOS+ neurons from the tdTomato+ population to the tdTomato- population (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The preferential recruitment of EE-activated neurons by learning is significantly reduced in both WT and Fmr1 KO mice when EE-activated neurons are inhibited by DREADD.
source: As a result, the preferential recruitment of EE-activated neurons by learning is significantly reduced in both WT and Fmr1 KO mice (the preference is not completely eliminated because inhibitory DREADD only induces modest hyperpolarization but does not completely shut down neuronal activity [Roth, 2016]).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5E and citation to Roth, 2016.

claim: Inhibitory DREADD only induces modest hyperpolarization but does not completely shut down neuronal activity.
source: As a result, the preferential recruitment of EE-activated neurons by learning is significantly reduced in both WT and Fmr1 KO mice (the preference is not completely eliminated because inhibitory DREADD only induces modest hyperpolarization but does not completely shut down neuronal activity [Roth, 2016]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Roth, 2016.

claim: When EE-activated neurons are inhibited by DREADD, new population of neurons that were not activated by EE (tdTomato-) could be engaged to support the demand of learning.
source: Taken together, the results so far suggest that when EE-activated neurons are inhibited by DREADD, new population of neurons that were not activated by EE (tdTomato-) could be engaged to support the demand of learning.
evidence: This is an inference based on the shift of FOS+ neurons from tdTomato+ to tdTomato- population shown in Figure 5E.

claim: DREADD-expressing WT and Fmr1 KO mice showed normal freezing during and after intensive fear conditioning training.
source: DREADD-expressing WT and Fmr1 KO mice showed normal freezing during and after intensive fear conditioning training (Figure 5G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The context memory rescue observed in EE-experienced Fmr1 KO mice was abolished by inhibiting EE engaged neurons.
source: Interestingly, the context memory rescue observed in EE-experienced Fmr1 KO mice was abolished by inhibiting EE engaged neurons, shown as significantly decreased freezing levels compared to wild-type mice (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: CNO injection itself showed no effect to animal's locomotion.
source: CNO injection itself showed no effect to animal's locomotion (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D) or freezing behavior (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: CNO injection itself showed no effect to animal's freezing behavior.
source: CNO injection itself showed no effect to animal's locomotion (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D) or freezing behavior (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–G.

claim: Inhibition of EE-activated neurons in wild-type mice have no significant effect on fear memory recall.
source: Inhibition of EE-activated neurons in wild-type mice have no significant effect on fear memory recall, indicated by comparable freezing levels during context memory test (p=0.1809 when comparing wild-type group freezing levels between Figures 5H and 3C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of data from Figure 5H and 3C.

claim: EE experience, through its direct impact on CA1 neurons, improves engram reactivation accuracy and rescues memory encoding in Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that EE experience, through its direct impact on CA1 neurons, improves engram reactivation accuracy and rescues memory encoding in Fmr1 KO mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined results from chemogenetic inhibition experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Synaptic plasticity has long been thought as the cellular mechanism of learning and memory.
source: Synaptic plasticity has long been thought as the cellular mechanism of learning and memory (Hebb, 1949).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hebb, 1949.

claim: Neural ensemble theory proposed by Donald O. Hebb hypothesized that learned associations are stored in a population of neurons.
source: Neural ensemble theory proposed by Donald O. Hebb hypothesized that learned associations are stored in a population of neurons, which is achieved through synaptic plasticity development during and after learning.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from Hebb's theory.

claim: Learned associations are achieved through synaptic plasticity development during and after learning.
source: Neural ensemble theory proposed by Donald O. Hebb hypothesized that learned associations are stored in a population of neurons, which is achieved through synaptic plasticity development during and after learning.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from Hebb's theory.

claim: Reactivation of engram cells elicits memory recall.
source: Reactivation of these neurons in the ensemble, often referred to as the engram cells, elicits memory recall (Josselyn and Tonegawa, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Josselyn and Tonegawa, 2020.

claim: Optogenetic activation and inactivation of learning-activated neural ensembles leads to facilitation and impairment of memory recall, respectively.
source: In these studies, optogenetic activation and inactivation of learning-activated neural ensembles leads to facilitation and impairment of memory recall, respectively (Roy et al., 2016; Tanaka et al., 2014), supporting the idea that memory traces are stored in engram cells and that their reactivation is critical for memory recall.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Roy et al., 2016 and Tanaka et al., 2014.

claim: Memory traces are stored in engram cells.
source: In these studies, optogenetic activation and inactivation of learning-activated neural ensembles leads to facilitation and impairment of memory recall, respectively (Roy et al., 2016; Tanaka et al., 2014), supporting the idea that memory traces are stored in engram cells and that their reactivation is critical for memory recall.
evidence: This is an inference based on optogenetic studies cited (Roy et al., 2016; Tanaka et al., 2014).

claim: Reactivation of engram cells is critical for memory recall.
source: In these studies, optogenetic activation and inactivation of learning-activated neural ensembles leads to facilitation and impairment of memory recall, respectively (Roy et al., 2016; Tanaka et al., 2014), supporting the idea that memory traces are stored in engram cells and that their reactivation is critical for memory recall.
evidence: This is an inference based on optogenetic studies cited (Roy et al., 2016; Tanaka et al., 2014).

claim: Successful reactivation of CA1 engram during memory recall test is essential for normal fear memory retrieval.
source: In this study, we applied these approaches to investigate the mechanism underlying cognition deficits in the FXS mouse model. We show that successful reactivation of CA1 engram during memory recall test, which is essential for normal fear memory retrieval, is impaired in Fmr1 KO mice, and that the recall efficacy is positively correlated with behavioral performances.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between engram reactivation and behavioral performance shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The recall efficacy is positively correlated with behavioral performances.
source: In this study, we applied these approaches to investigate the mechanism underlying cognition deficits in the FXS mouse model. We show that successful reactivation of CA1 engram during memory recall test, which is essential for normal fear memory retrieval, is impaired in Fmr1 KO mice, and that the recall efficacy is positively correlated with behavioral performances.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Learning-activated neurons in hippocampal CA1 are preferentially reactivated during memory recall.
source: Using well-established activity-dependent genetic labeling method, we showed that learning-activated neurons in hippocampal CA1 are indeed preferentially reactivated during memory recall, and that the efficacy of this engram reactivation is positively correlated with behavioral performances.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The efficacy of engram reactivation is positively correlated with behavioral performances.
source: Using well-established activity-dependent genetic labeling method, we showed that learning-activated neurons in hippocampal CA1 are indeed preferentially reactivated during memory recall, and that the efficacy of this engram reactivation is positively correlated with behavioral performances.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Reduced efficacy of neuronal ensemble reactivation correlates with reduced performance levels in fear memory recall test in Fmr1 KO mice.
source: In the Fmr1 KO mice, reduced efficacy of neuronal ensemble reactivation correlates with reduced performance levels in fear memory recall test.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E and 2F.

claim: Memory formation requires persistent changes at synapses that often involve new protein synthesis.
source: Memory formation requires persistent changes at synapses that often involve new protein synthesis (Ryan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ryan et al., 2015.

claim: Altered protein synthesis-dependent synaptic plasticity is a signature phenotype in the Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Given FMRP's function as an RNA-binding protein that regulates the synthesis of many synaptic plasticity-related proteins (Darnell and Klann, 2013), and altered protein synthesis-dependent synaptic plasticity is a signature phenotype in the Fmr1 KO mice (Huber et al., 2002), it is conceivable that the cognitive deficit observed in Fmr1 KO mice is due to defective transformation of transient learning-induced neuronal activation into lasting memory traces.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Huber et al., 2002.

claim: The cognitive deficit observed in Fmr1 KO mice is due to defective transformation of transient learning-induced neuronal activation into lasting memory traces.
source: Given FMRP's function as an RNA-binding protein that regulates the synthesis of many synaptic plasticity-related proteins (Darnell and Klann, 2013), and altered protein synthesis-dependent synaptic plasticity is a signature phenotype in the Fmr1 KO mice (Huber et al., 2002), it is conceivable that the cognitive deficit observed in Fmr1 KO mice is due to defective transformation of transient learning-induced neuronal activation into lasting memory traces.
evidence: This is a speculation based on FMRP's function and observed phenotypes.

claim: Despite normal performance during learning, Fmr1 KO mice show impaired engram reactivation during memory recall.
source: Indeed, our results show that despite the normal performance during learning, measured as freezing levels during and immediately after fear conditioning training and total number of neurons activated during learning and memory recall, Fmr1 KO mice show impaired engram reactivation during memory recall.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 1, 2C, 2D, and 2E.

claim: The deficits in memory recall most likely occur during the period of memory consolidation after learning.
source: Thus, we concluded that the deficits in memory recall most likely occur during the period of memory consolidation after learning, when development of synaptic plasticity supports changes in network connectivity and memory trace formation.
evidence: This is an inference based on normal learning but impaired recall shown in Figure 1.

claim: During spatial exploration, hippocampal CA1 places cells in WT and Fmr1 KO mice exhibit similar firing rates.
source: This is consistent with findings from a previous study showing that during spatial exploration, although hippocampal CA1 places cells in WT and Fmr1 KO mice exhibit similar firing rates, those in FXS mice showed reduced specificity and impaired stability (Arbab et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Arbab et al., 2018.

claim: Hippocampal CA1 place cells in FXS mice showed reduced specificity and impaired stability during spatial exploration.
source: This is consistent with findings from a previous study showing that during spatial exploration, although hippocampal CA1 places cells in WT and Fmr1 KO mice exhibit similar firing rates, those in FXS mice showed reduced specificity and impaired stability (Arbab et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Arbab et al., 2018.

claim: EE rescued fear memory recall in Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Our results showed that not only EE rescued fear memory recall in Fmr1 KO mice, but also restored engram reactivation accuracy in these mice, suggesting that the memory consolidation process was restored after EE.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: EE restored engram reactivation accuracy in Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Our results showed that not only EE rescued fear memory recall in Fmr1 KO mice, but also restored engram reactivation accuracy in these mice, suggesting that the memory consolidation process was restored after EE.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The memory consolidation process was restored after EE in Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Our results showed that not only EE rescued fear memory recall in Fmr1 KO mice, but also restored engram reactivation accuracy in these mice, suggesting that the memory consolidation process was restored after EE.
evidence: This is an inference based on restored engram reactivation and memory recall shown in Figure 3.

claim: Multiple mechanisms have been proposed that may contribute to EE-mediated memory improvement, including enhanced neurogenesis.
source: Multiple mechanisms have been proposed that may contribute to EE-mediated memory improvement, including enhanced neurogenesis (Kempermann et al., 1997), increased dendritic density and complexity (Faherty et al., 2003), changes in synaptic protein expression (Hüttenrauch et al., 2016; Nithianantharajah et al., 2004) and neurotrophic factors (Bekinschtein et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kempermann et al., 1997.

claim: Multiple mechanisms have been proposed that may contribute to EE-mediated memory improvement, including increased dendritic density and complexity.
source: Multiple mechanisms have been proposed that may contribute to EE-mediated memory improvement, including enhanced neurogenesis (Kempermann et al., 1997), increased dendritic density and complexity (Faherty et al., 2003), changes in synaptic protein expression (Hüttenrauch et al., 2016; Nithianantharajah et al., 2004) and neurotrophic factors (Bekinschtein et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Faherty et al., 2003.

claim: Multiple mechanisms have been proposed that may contribute to EE-mediated memory improvement, including changes in synaptic protein expression.
source: Multiple mechanisms have been proposed that may contribute to EE-mediated memory improvement, including enhanced neurogenesis (Kempermann et al., 1997), increased dendritic density and complexity (Faherty et al., 2003), changes in synaptic protein expression (Hüttenrauch et al., 2016; Nithianantharajah et al., 2004) and neurotrophic factors (Bekinschtein et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hüttenrauch et al., 2016 and Nithianantharajah et al., 2004.

claim: Multiple mechanisms have been proposed that may contribute to EE-mediated memory improvement, including changes in neurotrophic factors.
source: Multiple mechanisms have been proposed that may contribute to EE-mediated memory improvement, including enhanced neurogenesis (Kempermann et al., 1997), increased dendritic density and complexity (Faherty et al., 2003), changes in synaptic protein expression (Hüttenrauch et al., 2016; Nithianantharajah et al., 2004) and neurotrophic factors (Bekinschtein et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bekinschtein et al., 2011.

claim: Changes induced by EE may, directly or indirectly, lead to enhanced network function and synaptic plasticity.
source: These changes may, directly or indirectly, lead to enhanced network function and synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is a speculation about how EE-induced changes affect brain function.

claim: Enhanced sensory, motor and social experience during EE may support prolonged behaviorally meaningful patterns of neural activity.
source: Additionally, enhanced sensory, motor and social experience during EE may support prolonged behaviorally meaningful patterns of neural activity, which may shift Hebbian plasticity rules.
evidence: This is a speculation about how EE affects neural activity patterns.

claim: Prolonged behaviorally meaningful patterns of neural activity may shift Hebbian plasticity rules.
source: Additionally, enhanced sensory, motor and social experience during EE may support prolonged behaviorally meaningful patterns of neural activity, which may shift Hebbian plasticity rules.
evidence: This is a speculation about how neural activity patterns affect plasticity.

claim: Deficits in Hebbian plasticity have been widely reported in FXS models.
source: Deficits in Hebbian plasticity have been widely reported in FXS models (Huber et al., 2002; Lauterborn et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huber et al., 2002 and Lauterborn et al., 2007.

claim: mGluR-dependent LTD are enhanced, but not absent, in both hippocampus and cerebellum of Fmr1 KO mice.
source: mGluR-dependent LTD are enhanced, but not absent, in both hippocampus and cerebellum of Fmr1 KO mice (Hou et al., 2006; Huber et al., 2002; Koekkoek et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hou et al., 2006; Huber et al., 2002; Koekkoek et al., 2005.

claim: LTP impairment in Fmr1 KO mice depends on the age and strain of mice, and is induction protocol-dependent.
source: Studies investigating hippocampal and cortical LTP in Fmr1 KO mice showed that LTP impairment depends on the age and strain of mice, and is induction protocol-dependent (Lauterborn et al., 2007; Martin et al., 2016; Paradee et al., 1999), largely suggesting that the LTP expression mechanism is intact in Fmr1 KO mice, and that the observed deficits reflect an altered threshold for LTP induction (Desai et al., 2006; Meredith et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lauterborn et al., 2007; Martin et al., 2016; Paradee et al., 1999.

claim: The LTP expression mechanism is intact in Fmr1 KO mice.
source: Studies investigating hippocampal and cortical LTP in Fmr1 KO mice showed that LTP impairment depends on the age and strain of mice, and is induction protocol-dependent (Lauterborn et al., 2007; Martin et al., 2016; Paradee et al., 1999), largely suggesting that the LTP expression mechanism is intact in Fmr1 KO mice, and that the observed deficits reflect an altered threshold for LTP induction (Desai et al., 2006; Meredith et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference based on the variable nature of LTP deficits and citations to Desai et al., 2006; Meredith et al., 2007.

claim: The observed LTP deficits in Fmr1 KO mice reflect an altered threshold for LTP induction.
source: Studies investigating hippocampal and cortical LTP in Fmr1 KO mice showed that LTP impairment depends on the age and strain of mice, and is induction protocol-dependent (Lauterborn et al., 2007; Martin et al., 2016; Paradee et al., 1999), largely suggesting that the LTP expression mechanism is intact in Fmr1 KO mice, and that the observed deficits reflect an altered threshold for LTP induction (Desai et al., 2006; Meredith et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Desai et al., 2006 and Meredith et al., 2007.

claim: The fact that EE can rescue fear conditioning performance in Fmr1 KO mice supports the notion that basic signaling mechanisms underlying some forms of Hebbian plasticity (e.g. LTP) essential for fear memory encoding may be intact.
source: The fact that EE can rescue fear conditioning performance in Fmr1 KO mice supports the notion that basic signaling mechanisms underlying some forms of Hebbian plasticity (e.g. LTP) essential for fear memory encoding may be intact, but that the induction rules for these essential forms of plasticity have been changed in Fmr1 KOs due to altered non-Hebbian plasticity (i.e. homeostatic synaptic plasticity) (Sarti et al., 2013; Soden and Chen, 2010; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue effect of EE shown in Figure 3.

claim: The induction rules for essential forms of plasticity have been changed in Fmr1 KOs due to altered non-Hebbian plasticity (i.e. homeostatic synaptic plasticity).
source: The fact that EE can rescue fear conditioning performance in Fmr1 KO mice supports the notion that basic signaling mechanisms underlying some forms of Hebbian plasticity (e.g. LTP) essential for fear memory encoding may be intact, but that the induction rules for these essential forms of plasticity have been changed in Fmr1 KOs due to altered non-Hebbian plasticity (i.e. homeostatic synaptic plasticity) (Sarti et al., 2013; Soden and Chen, 2010; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on altered homeostatic plasticity cited (Sarti et al., 2013; Soden and Chen, 2010; Zhang et al., 2018).

claim: Animals raised in an EE environment exhibit enhanced Hebbian plasticity.
source: Indeed, it has been shown that animals raised in an EE environment exhibit enhanced Hebbian plasticity (Artola et al., 2006; Duffy et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Artola et al., 2006 and Duffy et al., 2001.

claim: The short EE protocol used in this study has been shown to alter Hebbian plasticity threshold in the hippocampus.
source: The short EE protocol used in this study has also been shown to alter Hebbian plasticity threshold in the hippocampus (Hsu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hsu et al., 2019.

claim: When the activity of EE-engaged neurons is dampened chemogenetically, the improvement in both engram activation accuracy and fear memory recall is abolished.
source: Importantly, when the activity of EE-engaged neurons is dampened chemogenetically, the improvement in both engram activation accuracy and fear memory recall is abolished.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5E and 5H.

claim: Neuronal activation during EE experience is instrumental toward facilitating learning-dependent development of synaptic plasticity through modification of synaptic states and/or circuit properties.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that neuronal activation during EE experience is instrumental toward facilitating learning-dependent development of synaptic plasticity through modification of synaptic states and/or circuit properties.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined results from EE and chemogenetic experiments shown in Figures 3-5.

claim: Neuronal excitability has been shown as a key factor in memory allocation.
source: Neuronal excitability has been shown as a key factor in memory allocation (Yiu et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2009), EE-activated neurons may have higher excitability due to their engagement in EE (Malik and Chattarji, 2012; Valero-Aracama et al., 2015), and thus are more likely to participate in subsequent learning (Lisman et al., 2018; Sekeres et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yiu et al., 2014 and Zhou et al., 2009.

claim: EE-activated neurons may have higher excitability due to their engagement in EE.
source: Neuronal excitability has been shown as a key factor in memory allocation (Yiu et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2009), EE-activated neurons may have higher excitability due to their engagement in EE (Malik and Chattarji, 2012; Valero-Aracama et al., 2015), and thus are more likely to participate in subsequent learning (Lisman et al., 2018; Sekeres et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to Malik and Chattarji, 2012 and Valero-Aracama et al., 2015.

claim: EE-activated neurons are more likely to participate in subsequent learning.
source: Neuronal excitability has been shown as a key factor in memory allocation (Yiu et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2009), EE-activated neurons may have higher excitability due to their engagement in EE (Malik and Chattarji, 2012; Valero-Aracama et al., 2015), and thus are more likely to participate in subsequent learning (Lisman et al., 2018; Sekeres et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4E and citations to Lisman et al., 2018 and Sekeres et al., 2010.

claim: EE-induced bias in neuronal activation during learning is very similar between WT and Fmr1 KO mice.
source: It is interesting that EE-induced bias in neuronal activation during learning is very similar between WT and Fmr1 KO mice, suggesting that this process is independent of FMRP expression.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The process of EE-induced bias in neuronal activation during learning is independent of FMRP expression.
source: It is interesting that EE-induced bias in neuronal activation during learning is very similar between WT and Fmr1 KO mice, suggesting that this process is independent of FMRP expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on similar bias in WT and KO mice shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Repeated and behaviorally relevant activation during EE induces changes in Fmr1 KO neurons that facilitates development of synaptic plasticity during learning, allowing normal memory consolidation to occur.
source: First, through a cell-autonomous process, repeated and behaviorally relevant activation during EE induces changes in Fmr1 KO neurons that facilitates development of synaptic plasticity during learning, allowing normal memory consolidation to occur.
evidence: This is a speculation about one possible mechanism for EE's effect.

claim: CA1 pyramidal neurons are heterogeneous in their development, gene expression patterns, anatomy, and function.
source: A second possibility is based on the observation that CA1 pyramidal neurons are heterogeneous in their development, gene expression patterns, anatomy, and function (Danielson et al., 2016; Mizuseki et al., 2011; Soltesz and Losonczy, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Danielson et al., 2016; Mizuseki et al., 2011; Soltesz and Losonczy, 2018.

claim: EE experience may preferentially activate a subset of CA1 neurons that are more effective in contextual memory encoding.
source: Thus, EE experience, due to its nature in promoting spatial navigation among other features, may preferentially activate a subset of CA1 neurons that are more effective in contextual memory encoding.
evidence: This is a speculation about another possible mechanism for EE's effect.

claim: EE experience in Fmr1 KO mice may result in a significant shift in the subtypes of CA1 neurons recruited during learning toward better contextual memory encoding.
source: Given our observation that EE-activated neurons are more likely to participate in subsequent learning, EE experience in Fmr1 KO mice may result in a significant shift in the subtypes of CA1 neurons recruited during learning toward better contextual memory encoding, thus improving memory recall in the Fmr1 KO mice.
evidence: This is a speculation based on preferential recruitment of EE-activated neurons shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Memory recall requires accessing the neural ensembles that constitute the memory engrams.
source: It is generally agreed that memory recall requires accessing the neural ensembles that constitute the memory engrams (Frankland et al., 2019; Tonegawa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Frankland et al., 2019 and Tonegawa et al., 2015.

claim: Memory engram reactivation is a non-random process that occurs significantly above chance level of neural ensemble reactivation.
source: Agreeing with many studies conducted in several brain regions including hippocampus (Denny et al., 2014; Kitamura et al., 2017; Nakazawa et al., 2016; Tanaka et al., 2014; Tayler et al., 2013; Zelikowsky et al., 2014), our data support the notion that memory engram reactivation is a non-random process that occurs significantly above chance level of neural ensemble reactivation.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2E and citations to multiple studies.

claim: The overall reactivation percentage never approaches 100% (roughly 10–40%, depending on the region, labeling approaches and behavioral paradigms).
source: However, these studies, including ours, also show that the overall reactivation percentage never approaches 100% (roughly 10–40%, depending on the region, labeling approaches and behavioral paradigms) (Tanaka et al., 2014; Tayler et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2E and citations to Tanaka et al., 2014 and Tayler et al., 2013.

claim: Reactivation of a fraction of memory ensemble is sufficient to produce full memory recall.
source: Just as Hebb predicted (Hebb, 1949), reactivation of a fraction of memory ensemble is sufficient to produce full memory recall.
evidence: This is based on Hebb's prediction and supported by citation to Hebb, 1949.

claim: Memory engram is flexible and dynamic.
source: First, memory engram is flexible and dynamic. There is potential built-in redundancy in the mechanism to ensure full memory recall by a partial presentation of cues (or partial usage of available cues).
evidence: This is a speculation about the nature of memory engrams.

claim: There is potential built-in redundancy in the mechanism to ensure full memory recall by a partial presentation of cues.
source: First, memory engram is flexible and dynamic. There is potential built-in redundancy in the mechanism to ensure full memory recall by a partial presentation of cues (or partial usage of available cues).
evidence: This is a speculation about memory mechanisms.

claim: Such redundancy ensures reliable behavioral responses in face of the less reliable sensory world.
source: Such redundancy ensures reliable behavioral responses in face of the less reliable sensory world (e.g. seasonal changes of scenery in the same location of the woods), thus increasing the chance of survival for the animals.
evidence: This is a speculation about the adaptive value of redundancy in memory systems.

claim: Imperfect genetic labeling may contribute (at least partly) to the perceived imperfection of memory engram reactivation.
source: A second possibility is that imperfect genetic labeling may contribute (at least partly) to the perceived imperfection of memory engram reactivation.
evidence: This is a speculation about technical limitations of current methods.

claim: The current IEG promoter approach may 'over-tag' or 'under-tag' the engrams.
source: With a relatively broad labeling time window (ranging from a few hours to several days [DeNardo and Luo, 2017]) and varied IEGs induction profiles in different cell-types (Cruz et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2020), the current IEG promoter approach may 'over-tag' or 'under-tag' the engrams, contributing to imperfect alignment between neural ensemble activation during learning and its reactivation during memory recall.
evidence: This is a speculation about technical limitations supported by citations to DeNardo and Luo, 2017; Cruz et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2020.

claim: Two different IEG-labeled ensembles act in a push-and-pull manner to ensure a balance between memory discrimination and generalization.
source: A recent study examining the different aspects of hippocampal memory engram (Sun et al., 2020) provides an excellent example in which two different IEG-labeled ensembles act in a push-and-pull manner to ensure a balance between memory discrimination and generalization.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sun et al., 2020.

claim: Majority of AAV-Fos-TRAP labeled neurons within the CA1 pyramidal layer are excitatory neurons as greater than 94% of them are positive for CaMKII staining.
source: Additional analysis indicates that majority of AAV-Fos-TRAP labeled neurons within the CA1 pyramidal layer are excitatory neurons as greater than 94% of them are positive for CaMKII staining (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F.
